segments.text: Verse 4
and there is none comparable to Him.”[1]
The surah closes by denying that anyone is comparable to Allah:
and there is none comparable to Him.”[1]
He has no counterpart or equal in His essence, attributes, or actions.
His words
Do you know anyone equal to Him?

have been explained as asking whether anyone knows a rival or a likeness to Him. The answer that settles in the heart of someone who worships Allah alone is that he knows no counterpart to his Lord to whom he could turn instead.
Revelation has taught him this foundation:
There is nothing like unto Him[1]
. So it is wrong to approach Allah’s names and attributes by measuring them against human circumstances, then reject whatever one cannot imagine a created being possessing.
One form of this error is to imagine that what is hidden from people is hidden from Allah, as in the answer to those who spoke privately about concealing what they knew:
Do they not know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal?
Another is to make belief in the Creator depend on seeing and touching, as people do with idols. The Children of Israel said,
we will never believe you until we see Allah openly
, and, on another occasion,
make for us a god just as they have gods.
The forms of the error change, but its root remains the same: subjecting knowledge of Allah to what people are accustomed to in created beings.

Sincere devotion, by contrast, receives what Allah has told us about Himself while affirming that He has no likeness. It neither invents attributes for Him nor denies Him a perfection because human beings cannot attain it.
Knowing that He has no equal is not remote from the heart’s needs. It ends the search for another god to provide what one seeks from Allah, or for a power that could force Allah to do its bidding.

The meanings of the surah therefore unfold in one direction: you know that He is One, so you turn to Him with your needs; then you learn that He has no child, parent, or counterpart, so your worship is not divided among different beings, each imagined to control a share of your affairs.
The Quran illustrates the effect of this oneness through its comparison of
a slave owned by several quarrelsome masters, and a slave owned by only one master
. The first is pulled by conflicting demands: scarcely has he satisfied one before another presses him. The second knows whom he serves.

Likewise, a heart that attaches its fears and hopes to everyone and every means becomes scattered and exhausted. In His mercy, Allah commanded it to worship Him alone, rather than carry the burden of pleasing many gods.

Gathering one’s concerns around Allah becomes a way out of this fragmentation. Knowing His oneness becomes a foundation for obedience, reassurance, and referring to His Book for judgment, rather than a statement detached from life.
One subtle point in the order of the Quran’s closing surahs is that this knowledge is followed by seeking refuge. Al-Falaq opens with
Say, “I seek refuge with the Lord of the daybreak,
Then An-Nas opens with
Say, “I seek refuge with the Lord of mankind,

The reader has passed through accounts of created beings and seen their weakness, and accounts of deliverance, victory, and mercy, learning who holds all of this in His hands. Once certain of the One, the Eternal Refuge, he brings his fear of evil to Him.

In Al-Falaq he seeks refuge from the evil of what Allah has created, from the evil of night as it falls, from those who blow on knots, and from the envier; in An-Nas he seeks refuge from the retreating whisperer who corrupts the heart from within.
These two surahs do not turn to a subject separate from Allah’s oneness. They show the fruit of knowing the One who has no equal.
The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, told ‘Uqbah ibn ‘Amir about these two surahs:
use them when seeking refuge in Allah, for no one can use anything to compare with them for the purpose.
The believer thus turns to his Lord with the words He taught him, attentive to their meaning.

Holding fast to the Quran does not mean a person will never be harmed. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, faced plots and envy, and the harm he suffered from magic is established. Of those filled with rage on hearing the Reminder, the Quran says:
The disbelievers would almost strike you down with their malicious gazes when they hear the Reminder
The believer needs to know to whom to turn when harm confronts him, rather than assume that merely following the path of truth will prevent harm from occurring.

This is why an attentive heart and certainty matter when seeking refuge. A person should not recite his Lord’s names while heedless of the One he is calling on, then treat the recitation as words that work by themselves.
An unattributed saying illustrates the point:
The staff depends on its wielder, and Al-Fatihah on its reciter

. Just as an instrument’s effectiveness cannot be separated from the state of the person using it, seeking refuge cannot be separated from the sincerity of the person seeking it and his attachment to Allah.
Allah is the One who determines relief and its timing. A servant does not set the moment of the answer, even when sincere in his supplication.

Seeking refuge with the Lord of daybreak reminds him of his Lord’s nurturing care and gentle governance. Relief may come gradually, as morning gradually emerges from night. So keep turning to Him, without making the soundness of your devotion depend on the disappearance of what troubles you at the moment you choose.

In this way you reach the end of the Quran with a belief to live by: your Lord has no counterpart to whom you could turn instead, and your heart can never do without His mercy, guidance, and protection.

publisherNotes.text: [1] The Prophet (ﷺ) says that reading this surah (surat al-Ikhlās) equals reading one third of the Qur’an. [Al-Bukhāri and Muslim]
[1] In His essence, His attributes, or His deeds.
